Flooding Disrupts South Korea’s Electric Utilities Industry; SGC Energy Co Ltd Among Those Affected

Flooding caused by days of torrential monsoon rains is disrupting operations across South Korea’s electric utilities industry, with power generation and transmission sites in several provinces reporting damage and outages. The event, which began late last week and continues as of Monday, has affected major facilities including those operated by SGC Energy Co Ltd and other utilities, raising concerns about potential supply instability if the situation persists.

According to the Korea Electric Utilities Association, water levels on the Nakdong and Han rivers have surged to their highest in more than a decade, inundating low-lying thermal and hydroelectric plants. SGC Energy Co Ltd confirmed on Sunday that its Gyeonggi Province generation facility suspended operations after floodwaters breached protective barriers, submerging key equipment. Emergency crews have been deployed to pump water from the site, but restoration timelines remain uncertain.

“Our priority is the safety of our employees and the protection of critical infrastructure,” an SGC Energy Co Ltd spokesperson said. “We are working closely with authorities to assess the extent of the damage and implement recovery measures, but the ongoing rainfall is hampering these efforts.”

Transmission lines linking several southern plants to the national grid have also been impacted by landslides and submerged access roads, complicating repair work. A spokesperson for the Korea Electric Utilities Association noted, “We are seeing significant logistical challenges, with many routes for maintenance teams impassable due to flooding. This is delaying both damage assessment and restoration.”

Industry analysts warned that prolonged outages could strain South Korea’s electricity supply, particularly with summer demand near its peak. “If additional plants are forced offline, or if transmission constraints persist, the risk of regional shortages will rise,” said Kim Joon-ho, an energy sector analyst at Mirae Research Institute. “Generators may have to rely on reserve capacity or consider load reductions to maintain grid stability.”

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy has convened emergency meetings with utility companies to coordinate response efforts. As of Monday afternoon, authorities reported that over 600 megawatts of generation capacity had been temporarily idled due to flooding, with further disruptions possible depending on weather developments.

Union representatives called for enhanced safety protocols and rapid deployment of resources to affected plants. “The industry must be prepared for more frequent extreme weather events,” said Park Soo-min, a spokesperson for the Electric Utilities Workers’ Union. “Protecting workers and ensuring power supply continuity are both vital.”

With meteorologists forecasting continued heavy rainfall through the week, electric utilities across South Korea remain on high alert.
